first_impression.reaction: James's mum is Korean-Australian and she's already asked whether we'll do a pyebaek, so I Googled it. The opening describes the day as a sequence, not a postcard: 'It is a sequence: a gift box carried to the bride's family, gifts passed between two households, a ceremony, then a quieter room where the couple bow to the groom's family and try to catch a skirtful of dried fruit.' No 'fairytale', and it says it'll cover marrying in Korea or bringing it home. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Many Korean couples today hold a Western-style ceremony in a wedding hall, then change into hanbok for a short pyebaek with the groom's family.
journey.reaction: That's the answer I actually needed in one line. We don't have to choose between a 'normal' wedding and James's mum's side. Both, same day.

journey.quote: Gifts such as the ham, yedan, yemul and chukuigeum are settled between families, so agree what you will keep before any amounts are discussed.
journey.reaction: Practical and honest. That's a conversation I'd rather have early than discover at the engagement dinner.

journey.quote: Customs vary by family, region and faith, and no two Korean weddings run exactly alike.
journey.reaction: Good. It isn't pretending there's one correct version, which would get me in trouble with the in-laws.

journey.quote: If your families want one, agree early who carries it, what goes inside and who chooses it.
journey.reaction: Useful. James's groomsmen would love the noisy door bargaining, but I'd want to know first whether his mum expects it.

journey.section: 3. What a modern Korean wedding looks like in a wedding hall
journey.quote: For how public weddings look, see our round-up of [Korean stars who married in October 2026](/trending/korean-stars-married-october-2026).
journey.reaction: This one jars. Everything else reads like a serious guide, then there's a celebrity gossip link. Feels a bit tabloid for a brand I'd trust with a six-figure wedding.

journey.quote: The bride's robes are heavy and attendants guide her movements, so allow time in the run sheet.
journey.reaction: That's the kind of insider detail I look for. Someone has seen this run before.

journey.quote: If you are marrying away from Korea, ask whether a pair has been handed down in the family.
journey.reaction: Lovely, personal touch. I'll ask James's mum. The Joseon history above it I skimmed.

journey.quote: The layers take time, so brief your photographer and venue on extra dressing time and ask for a private room for the change.
journey.reaction: Exactly the logistics I'd forget. The museum garment descriptions are pretty but a lot to wade through when skimming.

journey.section: 8. Jujubes, chestnuts and carrying the bride
journey.quote: Both moments happen fast, so brief your photographer and keep a clear path around the table.
journey.reaction: Ha, good tip. This is the bit our friends will love, and it doesn't feel try-hard because it's the family's tradition, not a gimmick.

journey.quote: The rainy season usually runs from June to August, typhoon season from August to September, and heatwaves fall between June and September.
journey.reaction: Straight, specific, and it tells me when not to pick a date. That's honest trade-off territory.

journey.quote: For 2027 dates, recheck entry rules before the invitations go out.
journey.reaction: We're 14 months out, so this is us. Appreciate it being flagged rather than glossed.

journey.quote: Marriages in South Korea are registered at the local district office. As at November 2026, ask the district office and the Embassy:
journey.reaction: Clear on what's ours to sort, and the question list is handy. But this whole section is dense. As a lawyer I can follow it; my parents won't. And I'm left wondering whether anyone helps us chase this or it's entirely on us.

journey.quote: Dual nationality is recognised only in limited circumstances, and male Australian-Korean dual nationals of military age may need to complete military service.
journey.reaction: Didn't expect that, and it's genuinely important for James's cousins. This kind of frankness builds trust.

journey.section: Seoul and Jeju as places couples choose
journey.quote: Couples who marry in South Korea often choose Seoul, close to family, hotels and the city's wedding halls, or Jeju, the island to the south, for a smaller gathering by the sea.
journey.reaction: Nice framing, but it stops there. Half our guests would be flying in. Where do 70 people stay in Jeju, how do my grandparents get from Incheon to the island, and who's on the ground? That's the reason we'd hire someone.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia
journey.quote: Who will source the table, the screen and the hanbok, and who will set them up?
journey.reaction: Exactly the question I'd have. But the article asks it back at me rather than telling me whether the advisor can handle it.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia (advisor paragraph)
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the parts your families lead, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: Best line on the page for us. James's mum will lead the pyebaek, and 'single point of contact' answers who's accountable.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia (advisor paragraph)
journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Hidden costs and currency surprises, both addressed. Good.

journey.section: Planning your Korean wedding with us
journey.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a pyebaek at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want. Nothing is too early or too vague.
journey.reaction: Low pressure, right for where we are. And the link is right there this time.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned a Korean or Korean-Australian wedding with a pyebaek before? Is there a real one with a venue and date I can look at?
If we married in Seoul or Jeju, where would 60 to 90 guests stay, and who handles airport transfers for older relatives?
Can the Wedded Advisor source the pyebaek table, screen, dried fruit and hanbok hire in Australia, or is that on the family?
Does the advisor help coordinate the paperwork timeline with the Embassy and district office, even if the legal steps stay with us?
Who owns the run sheet on the day across the ceremony, the hanbok change and the pyebaek?

turn_offs_found.quote: For how public weddings look, see our round-up of [Korean stars who married in October 2026](/trending/korean-stars-married-october-2026).
turn_offs_found.why: Celebrity gossip link sits oddly in an otherwise serious, premium guide and cheapens it a little.

would_share_with: James's mum (the ham, yedan and yemul, the pyebaek at home, the wedding geese)
My parents (what a pyebaek is, chukuigeum, what to wear as a guest)

cta_reaction.why: Low pressure, a written AUD fee and a single point of contact are real pluses. But I want to see a real wedding where you've worked with a Korean family, and to know whether pyebaek setup and guest travel are in scope, so I'd read another post or two first.

top_3_changes: Link to a real Korean or Korean-Australian wedding from your pages, with venue and date, so I can see you've done this before.

Say plainly what the Wedded Advisor does for a pyebaek at home (sourcing the table, screen, hanbok, the quiet room) and for guests travelling to Seoul or Jeju (where they stay, transfers, who is on the ground).
Drop or replace the 'Korean stars who married' link; it undercuts the serious tone of the rest of the guide.
